name: Wei Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the data reporter at a small nonprofit news site that covers the region, funded by reader donations and a foundation grant. Most days I'm digging through planning applications, council spending records and inspection reports, and I use AI tools every day to search thousands of pages and flag the odd bits. Then I pick up the phone and go and knock on doors, because a spreadsheet never tells you why something happened. I love the hunt; what wears me out is that the grant only runs to the end of next year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens if the grant isn't renewed?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Then there are four of us looking for work in a region with basically one daily paper and a radio station. I live in a shared house with three other people, which is the only way I can afford rent on what we're paid. My savings would last about three weeks, so I try not to think about it too hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a really good research assistant and nothing more, and that's fine. I'd probably post a thread about how we used it to find the landlord with forty failed safety checks, because it did help with that. A spreadsheet never tells you why something happened, so the story was still us knocking on doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a world where AI is just a helpful tool suits me pretty well. I'm already ahead on the tools, so I'm a bit faster than most reporters my age. The real worry stays the grant, and AI fizzling out doesn't touch that either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools daily and teach the other three reporters my tricks for searching documents. I'd start a small paid newsletter on regional planning, maybe five pounds a month, to have some money that isn't tied to the grant. And I'd build a tiny buffer, even a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. A bit uneasy about the grant, but that's a problem I've lived with for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many people would pay five pounds for a planning newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe eighty to start, mostly local campaigners, architects and a few nosy councillors. That's not a living, but it's about a month's rent a year after costs. It would also prove there's demand if I ever had to go independent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's your boss, and how would they feel about the newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The editor is a former national reporter who started the site with her own savings. She'd be fine as long as I didn't scoop us with it. We'd probably agree the newsletter only covers routine planning lists, not investigations.

say: AI turned out to be a good **research assistant** and nothing more, which is fine.
He'd post about using it to find a landlord with **forty failed** safety checks.
think: A world where AI is just a **helpful tool** suits him, since he's already ahead.
The real worry stays the **grant**, which AI's fizzling out doesn't touch.
do: Teach the other three reporters his **document-search** tricks with AI.
Launch a **paid planning newsletter** at five pounds a month.
Build a small **buffer** of a few hundred pounds.
feel: **Fairly okay**, with familiar unease about whether the grant gets renewed.
S0.quote: A spreadsheet never tells you why something happened, so the story was still us knocking on doors.
fieldNote: Already an **everyday AI user**, so a plateau rewards him modestly.
His deeper worry is **grant funding**, which predates AI entirely.
Instinct to build a **side income** shows his comfort with risk.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily to search council and planning documents
Launch a five-pound monthly newsletter on regional planning
Save a few hundred pounds as an emergency buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be great for accountability journalism if we use it right, because one reporter can now read what used to take ten. I'd also say loudly that publishers shouldn't use it as an excuse to fire people. I'd be giving talks about it at every journalism meetup I could get into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the people who does fine, at least for a while. Reporters who can work with these tools will be wanted, and I'm one of them. What worries me is this. Being wanted might mean one of me doing the job of four, on the same low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a couple of simple tools for our newsroom, like an alert that flags unusual council contracts each week, and offer them to other small newsrooms for a fee. I'd push to set up a reporters' cooperative across the region so small outlets share tools and data. I'd also ask for a raise, because I'd be worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit of excitement mixed in. It's strange to feel both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do fine. Who wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reporters who mostly rewrite press releases, and there are a lot of them at the big regional chain. Also the subeditors. I've got friends in both and I'd feel guilty being the one who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money from selling tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, three months of savings, because I've never had that. Then maybe put a bit towards the cooperative idea. I wouldn't buy anything flashy; I'd just like not to panic every time the grant meeting comes up.

say: AI could be great for **accountability journalism**, letting one reporter read what took ten.
Publishers shouldn't use it as **an excuse** to fire people.
think: Reporters who work well with these tools will be **wanted**, and he's one of them.
Being wanted might mean **one person doing four** jobs on the same low pay.
do: Build a weekly **contract alert** tool and sell it to small newsrooms.
Push for a regional **reporters' cooperative** to share tools and data.
Ask for a **raise** based on his new value.
feel: **Uneasy** and a little excited at once, which feels strange to him.
S1.quote: Being wanted might mean one of me doing the job of four, on the same low pay.
fieldNote: Expects his own job to be **safe**, so unease, not anxiety, fits here.
Feels **guilt** at benefiting while friends who rewrite press releases lose out.
Turns his **progressive** views into a practical idea: a cooperative, not just protest.

steps.text: Build a weekly alert flagging unusual council contracts
Sell the contract alert tool to other small newsrooms
Organise a regional cooperative of small news outlets
Use tool income to build three months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public ownership of some of this, or at least strong public rules, because a handful of firms would control what everyone reads. I'd be campaigning for a public-interest AI for news, run like the public broadcaster. I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even the AI-savvy reporters get swept away by 2028. If the machine can do any thinking work, it doesn't need me to steer it for long. Knocking on doors is the hands-on bit, and maybe that buys three years until 2031, but I'd be one of very few people still paid to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the two years before it arrives making myself the person who goes out and gets the human side: the door-knocking, the court steps, the protests. I'd try to sell that to whoever's left, including AI news firms that need real reporting. I'd also move somewhere cheaper, maybe back to my dad's town, to cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one about tech, and this one scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your housemates the week AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that we should all sit down and work out who's earning what, because two of them work in call centres and they'd be gone even faster than me. We'd be planning together whether we liked it or not. I'd cook a big dinner and we'd go through the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell to AI news firms. Doesn't that clash with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, completely. I'd hate it. But I'd rather be the human in the loop feeding it true things than leave that to nobody.

say: We need **public rules** or ownership, so a few firms don't control what everyone reads.
He'd campaign for a **public-interest AI** for news, run like the public broadcaster.
think: Even **AI-savvy** reporters like him would be swept away by 2028.
**Door-knocking** is the hands-on bit, and might buy three years until 2031.
do: Specialise in **on-the-ground** reporting: doors, court steps and protests.
Sell that reporting to whoever's left, including **AI news firms**.
Move back to his **dad's town** to cut rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, even though he's usually the calm one about technology.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the human in the loop feeding it true things than leave that to nobody.
fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** early adopter expects to lose most of his income here.
He spots the **hands-on** edge of reporting as the only part that buys time.
Admits a sharp **politics clash** in working for AI news firms.

steps.text: Pitch on-the-ground reporting to surviving outlets and AI news firms
Move back to his dad's town to cut rent
Campaign for a public-interest AI news service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up public-interest newsrooms that use AI but stay accountable. I'd be writing proposals to foundations and councils, not just complaining. I'd say we have to design this, not just let it happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years gives me a real shot at building something. By 2031 I'd be thirty-two, with maybe a small business that combines AI research with human reporting. My reporting job as it is won't survive, but a small company built by reporters might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd turn the newsletter and the alert tool into a small company, with two other reporters as co-owners. I'd apply to every foundation fund for local news innovation. I'd keep my job at the nonprofit as long as the grant lasts, so I'm not risking rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an active way. There's a lot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier your savings would last three weeks. Is starting a company realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I keep the day job and don't spend anything I don't have. I wouldn't take a loan. It would be evenings and weekends, which I already do for fun anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd build something clever and then the big firms would just copy it for free. That's happened to small tech projects before. So I'd want it owned by the reporters and tied to real local relationships nobody can copy.

say: Five years is enough to set up **public-interest newsrooms** that use AI but stay accountable.
We have to **design** this change, not just let it happen.
think: Five years gives him **a real shot** at building something of his own.
His job as it is **won't survive**, but a version of it might.
do: Turn the newsletter and alert tool into a **reporter-owned** small company.
Apply to every **foundation fund** for local news innovation.
Keep the **nonprofit job** while the grant lasts, so rent stays covered.
feel: **Anxious** in an active way, with lots to do.
S3.quote: My reporting job as it is won't survive, but a small company built by reporters might.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his fear into an **enterprise plan**.
Careful with money: **no loans**, evenings and weekends only.
Worried big firms would **copy** small tools, so he leans on local relationships.

steps.text: Register a reporter-owned company with two colleagues
Apply to foundation funds for local news innovation
Keep the nonprofit data reporter job while the grant lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to rebuild local news properly, and if we fail it's a choice. I'd want public funding for local reporting written into law within the decade. I'd be loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly hopeful in this one. Ten years means I could grow the company slowly, get savings, and maybe even own a stake in something. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven and could have a team, not just a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do everything from the five-year picture but slower and with less risk. I'd take a short course in running a small business, and I'd start saving properly, aiming for three months in the first year. I'd also get on the board of the regional journalism association to shape how this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more good-uneasy than bad. Like before a big race you've trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've described lots of plans. Is there anything you'd hold off on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving in with my girlfriend, maybe. She lives two hours away and we keep talking about it. I'd want the business on its feet before I moved away from my patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be thinking about in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger sister, who's starting a journalism degree next year. I'd honestly tell my younger sister to pair a journalism degree with data or law. I'd feel bad if she trained for a job that's gone by the time she's twenty-five.

say: Ten years is plenty of time to **rebuild local news**, and failing would be a choice.
He wants **public funding** for local reporting written into law within the decade.
think: He's **fairly hopeful**, since a decade lets the company grow slowly.
By thirty-seven he could lead **a team**, not just hold a job.
do: Take a short course in **running a small business**.
Save towards **three months** of expenses in the first year.
Join the board of the regional **journalism association**.
feel: **Good-uneasy**, like the nerves before a race he's trained for.
S4.quote: I'd honestly tell my younger sister to pair a journalism degree with data or law.
fieldNote: The long runway makes him one of the **more hopeful** voices, despite thin savings.
AI is quietly **delaying** a move to live with his girlfriend.
Worry shifts to his **sister**, who's about to start journalism training.

steps.text: Take a short course in running a small business
Save towards three months of expenses this year
Delay moving in with his girlfriend until the business is steady
Join the board of the regional journalism association

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it wipes out even the advantage I've worked for, and there's no time to build anything. What would help is public funding for local journalism, and maybe a public-interest AI that small newsrooms can use for free. A safety net for people in their twenties too, because we have no savings to fall back on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people will still trust news at all. If AI can write anything, readers will want to know a real person checked it. I think that trust might be the most valuable thing a local reporter has left.

headlineQuote: If AI can write anything, readers will want to know a real person checked it.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old data reporter** at a grant-funded nonprofit news site, living in a shared house.
He uses **AI daily** and sees himself as one of the reporters who'd do fine in milder change.
He's **uneasy** in the milder pictures and AGI by 2036, but **alarmed** under AGI by 2028.
His plans centre on **reporter-owned** tools, a newsletter and a regional cooperative.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it erases the advantage he's built and leaves no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Public funding** for local journalism and a free public-interest AI for small newsrooms.
A **safety net** for people in their twenties with no savings.
